chapter_title: The Chapter of the Nazorean who questions the Teacher
chapter_note: This chapter contains NO cosmological-correspondential substrate. Teaching purity is 0.000. The entire chapter is an apologetic narrative: a Nazorean asks whether God is good or evil, and Mani argues via civic judge analogy that God is a judge who limits evil without being evil himself. The argument works through analogy from contemporary civic life to theology — no cosmic domain-to-domain mapping exists. Contains an explicit Gospel citation (¶10: Matt 6:21/Luke 12:34). The chapter is entirely composed of dialogue frame, editorial theological argument, and exhortation. It represents Manichaean apologetic composition, not a wrapper around older teaching.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Classic dialogue frame opening: 'Once again, it happened one time' + narrative setup introducing the Nazorean interlocutor and 'the apostle'. Purely formulaic.
Dialogue attribution ('The apostle speaks to him') followed by witty exchange about single vs. many words. Narrative banter, no teaching content.

The Nazorean's question: 'is he good or evil?' This is a theological/polemical question, NOT a substantive cosmological question about cosmic structure. It sets up an apologetic exchange, not a correspondential teaching sequence.

Heavy dialogue attribution ('Then says the apostle to that Nazorean'). Contains the key theological claim 'A judge is my God' — but this is a confessional/apologetic statement, not cosmological substrate.
The Nazorean's counter-argument using civic judge imagery (lashes, racks, chains, sword). This is philosophical rhetoric within the dialogue, drawing on contemporary civic life. No cosmic content.

Mani's theological response about the nature of judgment. Has dialogue attribution but substance is theological argument: 'the judge is not a man of wickedness, but rather the work counteracts wickedness.' This is apologetic theology, not cosmic mapping. The argument reasons from contemporary civic institutions.
Continuation of the judge analogy — righteous people have nothing to fear. 'Judge's seat' and civic imagery. Entirely theological argument from civic analogy, no cosmic domain mapping.

Continuation: the wicked bring punishment on themselves, the righteous receive recompense. Moral cause-and-effect theology. 'He shall set his wickedness upon his own head' — ethical teaching, not cosmological structure.

Explicit bridge from civic analogy to theology: 'Again, this also is the way of God. And he too is a judge of souls.' The word 'also' signals the editorial bridge. Mentions 'the devil', 'the truth and the knowledge' — theological vocabulary, not cosmological-correspondential substrate. Lacunae at end.

Contains explicit Gospel citation: 'Even as the saviour has said: Where your heart is, your treasure will come to be there' (Matt 6:21/Luke 12:34). This is a clear temporal marker — the citation enters via the NT. The passage applies the judge theology to eschatological judgment. 'Portion of the devil' — theological, not cosmological.
Theological conclusion: God does no evil, people condemn themselves. 'Gehenna of burning' — eschatological vocabulary from Jewish-Christian tradition, not cosmological substrate.
Eschatological promises: 'kingdom of light', 'life eternal', 'heirs'. Classic exhortation/devotional closure vocabulary. Rewards for 'people of good deeds' — moral application layer.
Summary conclusion returning to the 'judge' thesis. 'He shall not do what is evil; but rather as he limits the evil, he takes it away.' Wraps up the theological argument. No cosmological content.
